transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 43 minutes
Attendees: Samantha Li (Redwood AE), Dev Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (CTO - Artemis), Ethan Park (Lead ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Infra)
Shared: cost model spreadsheet link (sent in chat), Redwood batching guide (link)

[00:00] Samantha (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros - I'm Samantha, AE on the account. Dev here is our SE who's going to dig into the perf and costing. Maya, do you want to kick off with a bit of context about what Artemis is trying to do?

[00:18] Maya (Artemis): Yeah, sure. Thanks. So we're building a high-throughput summarization service for internal research - roughly 10k requests per hour in peak, average prompt length, you know, 400 tokens in and about 150 out. Latency needs are not ultra-low but we care about cost - we're trying to get per-user costs below a certain threshold. We're evaluating hosted vs running ourselves.

[00:36] Dev (Redwood SE): Cool makes sense. When you say cost you mean per-token cost and also infra overhead - how are you currently running?

[00:44] Ethan (Artemis): Right now it's on a mix - some inference on prem with a small GPU fleet, and some calls to a third-party API. Our internal ops team says the unit economics are spiking when traffic increases.

[00:54] Samantha: Yeah that's pretty common. Today's call is basically a cost-econ discovery - we want to understand your traffic profile, token mix, and budget so we can show scenarios: Hosted (pay-as-you-go), Dedicated reserved capacity, or Private (VPC/on-prem) and the tradeoffs.

[01:14] Maya: Perfect. On budget - we're aiming at a rough target of $0.0004 to $0.0006 per input token inclusive of infra. Is that realistic?

[01:23] Dev: Okay interesting that number. A lot depends on model choice and batching/caching. For context: our hosted per-token list pricing for the model family similar to gpt- style is X (we'll send exact), but effective unit cost can be ~2-5x lower with batching, continuous KV/prefix caching, and quantized models. With Dedicated reserved nodes you can push cost-per-token down further because of amortized GPU utilization.

[01:48] Liam: So what levers do we have? Batching seems obvious but does it increase latency? Our SLAs are 300-500 ms p95.

[01:56] Dev: Yes batching reduces cost-per-token by combining requests into larger micro-batches but it can add processing delay. Redwood's runtime supports latency-aware batching where we set a max-wait (e.g., 20 ms) and an adaptive batch size to hit SLOs. For your latency range it's doable - we usually see small batching windows that still keep p95 under 300-500 ms depending on sequence lengths.

[02:18] Ethan: And KV cache / prefix cache? Our use case has a lot of repeated contexts, we could cache previous summaries.

[02:26] Dev: KV caching is huge for repeated prefixes. If you have short-term repeated contexts, our prefix cache can return cached tokens or reuse KV cache to avoid re-computation. For summarization, if users re-run on similar docs, hit rates can be substantial. That can reduce compute by 30-70% depending on similarity.

[02:44] Maya: How reliable are those numbers? We can't assume cache hits in worst-case.

[02:50] Samantha: Totally - we plan for baseline and cache-boosted scenarios. We'll model best/expected/worst case in the spreadsheet. Usually customers plan budget with conservative cache hit assumptions (e.g., 10-20%) then see upside.

[03:04] Ethan: What about quantization? We saw some open-source 4-bit quantized models - is that supported?

[03:10] Dev: Yes, Redwood supports quantized variants and picks kernels accordingly. 4-bit QAT or post-training quant can reduce memory and improve throughput but there are tradeoffs in accuracy. Our Optimize tooling recommends quantization per workload and provides quality regression alerts tied to eval prompts.

[03:28] Liam: If we went Dedicated, what does pricing look like? We have some predictable peaks around monthly reporting periods.

[03:35] Samantha: Dedicated is reserved GPU capacity - you commit monthly or annually. The unit compute cost is lower and you get predictable throughput and isolation. We can run sizing based on your concurrency, tokens/sec, and burst needs and give a monthly cost + overage model. We'll include a Dedicated sizing sheet.

[03:53] Maya: And Private? We have compliance concerns - SOC2 and KMS.

[03:58] Samantha: Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you a customer-managed network and optional on-prem package. We integrate with KMS/HSM for key management and provide audit logs. For SOC2/ISO customers we also have enterprise support and contract add-ons. We'll share the security deck.

[04:13] Ethan: One practical question - when you say per-token pricing, do you bill for input and output tokens? Some providers bill both ways.

[04:19] Samantha: Yes, our hosted pricing bills for both input and output tokens, and we show effective per-inference cost in the model sheet. For Dedicated we typically price per GPU hour with an estimated token capacity overlay, and we provide effective per-token numbers for comparison.

[04:34] Dev: Also important: caching can change the billing picture. If a response is served entirely from cache and no new tokens are computed, the billable compute is lower. We'll map that in the scenarios.

[04:46] Maya: Any examples for a live workload? I want to see numbers.

[04:50] Dev: Sure - high level example: a mid-sized open LLM on hosted list price might be $0.002 per input token and $0.004 per output token - but with batching and cache hits, effective per-inference cost can drop to $0.0005-$0.001 in many cases. Dedicated can lower further depending on utilization. We'll put concrete examples in the spreadsheet.

[05:15] Ethan: What about throughput and tail latency when batching? If we need to scale to 10k rps in short bursts, do we auto-scale?

[05:22] Samantha: Hosted has autoscaling with multi-az fallback. Dedicated supports configurable autoscale policies and burst capacity. For very spiky bursts we often suggest a small Dedicated footprint plus hosted fallback, or setting burst capacity on Dedicated.

[05:37] Liam: What are typical RPS numbers per GPU for the models you're recommending?

[05:41] Dev: It varies by model and sequence length. For a 8k-token-optimized GPU and a 7B-ish model, you might get a few hundred token/sec effective throughput per GPU under optimized kernels; for larger models throughput drops. We'll include model-by-model profiles in the deck.

[05:58] Maya: Ok, let's talk risk. If we start Hosted and later move to Dedicated, how painful is that?

[06:05] Dev: We design the API and deployment to be consistent - same routes and model versions. Moving from Hosted to Dedicated is mostly a routing/config change and a migration of capacity; you can pin model versions and rollout policies so client-side changes are minimal. We do recommend a staged migration with canary traffic.

[06:23] Ethan: Great. For the pilot benchmark, what do you need from us?

[06:27] Samantha: If you can send 3 days of representative traffic (anonymized) and the prompt set, we can run the benchmark on Hosted and return cost and latency distributions. Also let us know the target SLOs.

[06:38] Ethan: We'll anonymize and share. Curious about tooling - you mentioned Optimize and quality regression alerts?

[06:45] Dev: Right - Redwood Optimize will surface batching and quantization recommendations and flags if output quality drifts versus your eval prompts. It's a way to balance cost and quality.

[06:56] Maya: Any blockers around data residency for EU data? We have EU customers and some data can't leave region.

[07:02] Samantha: We have regional hosting and Private deployments for strict residency. For Hosted we support region pinning for customers in EU. We'll note region-residency options in the follow-up.

[07:13] Liam: SSO and RBAC? We need integration into Okta and fine-grained permissions.

[07:18] Samantha: Yep - SSO/SAML, SCIM, and RBAC are supported on Dedicated and Private; hosted also supports SSO for orgs. We'll include the integration checklist.

[07:29] Ethan: Cool. From a numbers standpoint, if we assume 400 input + 150 output tokens per request, 10k reqs/hour peak, what's a rough monthly token volume?

[07:38] Dev: Quick math: that's 550 tokens per request * 10k reqs/hour * say 6 peak hours * 30 days = 550 * 10k * 6 * 30 = ~990M tokens per month in peak-window accounting. We'll validate with your real traffic but that indicates Dedicated could be cost-effective.

[07:58] Maya: Good to know. Please be conservative in the model.

[08:02] Samantha: Absolutely. We'll provide best/expected/worst row.

[08:06] Ethan: One last thing - do you provide token-level cost breakdown by route/model? We have a few microservices and want to see which routes are expensive.

[08:13] Dev: Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdown, per-route dashboards, and tracing. Customers use that to reassign budgets and identify heavy routes.

[08:22] Samantha: Alright, quick recap and next steps: we'll send the pricing spreadsheet, batching guide, and security deck today. Dev will kick off the benchmark once you share traffic. Follow-up call week of 2026-03-16 to review results. Anything else?

[08:38] Maya: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

[08:41] Ethan: Thanks.

[08:42] Liam: Thanks all.

Notes about transcription: occasional words were garbled (e.g., "K-V cache" transcribed as "kay vee cache"), small crosstalk when numbers were being recited.

References shared in chat: cost-model-spreadsheet.xlsx (link), redwood-batching-guide.pdf (link), security-deck.pdf (link).

End of transcript.
